# package syncobj

```go
import "github.com/otfabric/go-canopen/sync"
```

Package syncobj implements the CANopen SYNC object (CiA 301 7.2.5). It lives in the directory sync/ of the module but is named syncobj, so that it does not shadow the standard library's sync package where both are imported:

	import "github.com/otfabric/go-canopen/sync" // package syncobj

A [Producer](#type-producer) sends the SYNC message every communication cycle period (0x1006, µs) on the SYNC COB-ID (0x1005, produced when bit 30 is set), with a counter byte 1..overflow when the synchronous counter overflow value (0x1019) is 2..240. A [Consumer](#type-consumer) receives SYNC messages and reports them with their counter and the end of the synchronous window (0x1007), which is what synchronous PDOs are driven by: the pdo package's OnSyncWindow takes [Event.WindowEnd](#func-event-windowend) and enforces the window (synchronous TPDOs not sent and RPDOs not received within it are discarded); [Consumer.Window](#func-consumer-window) and [Consumer.InWindow](#func-consumer-inwindow) expose it.

CANopen FD (CiA 1301) keeps the SYNC protocol (0 or 1 data byte, default CAN-ID 080h) but carries it, like every protocol, in CAN FD frames: [WithFD](#func-withfd) makes the producer send CAN FD frames and the consumer accept them.

Timing: the producer uses a time.Ticker, so SYNC does not drift over time, but every message is subject to the scheduling latency of the Go runtime and the operating system (jitter typically in the tens to hundreds of microseconds on an idle system, more under load). Consumers timestamp SYNC with the frame's receive time when the transport reports one (SocketCAN does), which is closer to the bus than the handler call.

Long-running services have Start, which subscribes before it returns, and Close, which stops them and waits for their goroutine. Callbacks run on the service's goroutine and must not block for long.

### type Event

```go
type Event struct {
	// Counter is the SYNC counter (1..overflow), or 0 for a SYNC without
	// data.
	Counter uint8
	// Time is the frame's receive timestamp, or the time it was processed.
	// It carries a monotonic clock reading (see [Consumer]), so that the
	// window survives steps of the wall clock.
	Time time.Time
	// WindowEnd is the end of the synchronous window (Time + window
	// length), after which synchronous PDOs must not be sent any more;
	// zero when no window is configured.
	WindowEnd time.Time
	// LengthError reports a SYNC whose length does not match the
	// configured counter overflow value (0 bytes for 0, 1 byte otherwise);
	// CiA 301 has the node signal it with EMCY 0x8240. It is only checked
	// when the overflow value is known.
	LengthError bool
}
```

Event is a SYNC message a [Consumer](#type-consumer) received.

### type Option

```go
type Option func(*config)
```

Option configures a [Producer](#type-producer) or a [Consumer](#type-consumer). Each option names the services it applies to; the others ignore it.

#### func WithCOBID

```go
func WithCOBID(cob canopen.COBID) Option
```

WithCOBID sets the SYNC COB-ID (both services; default 0x080). Flag bits are ignored.

#### func WithDictionary

```go
func WithDictionary(d *od.Dictionary) Option
```

WithDictionary takes the parameters from a node's object dictionary and follows their changes: the COB-ID SYNC 0x1005 (bit 30: this node generates SYNC), the communication cycle period 0x1006 (µs), the synchronous window length 0x1007 (µs, consumer) and the synchronous counter overflow value 0x1019. It installs the write hooks CiA 301 requires: 0x1019 cannot change while the period is not 0 ([canopen.AbortDeviceState](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/otfabric/go-canopen#AbortDeviceState)) and accepts 0 and 2..240 only ([canopen.AbortInvalidValue](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/otfabric/go-canopen#AbortInvalidValue)); the CAN-ID of 0x1005 cannot change while the node generates SYNC ([canopen.AbortDeviceState](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/otfabric/go-canopen#AbortDeviceState)). Values wider than their object (possible only with a dictionary that declares them wider) are refused: a COB-ID write with [canopen.AbortInvalidValue](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/otfabric/go-canopen#AbortInvalidValue), at construction an error (unless an option overrides the value), and a later local change is ignored, as is a local change of 0x1019 to a value other than 0 and 2..240.

#### func WithFD

```go
func WithFD(brs bool) Option
```

WithFD selects CANopen FD (CiA 1301), which carries every protocol in CAN FD frames: a [Producer](#type-producer) sends SYNC as a CAN FD frame (with bit rate switching when brs is true) of the same 0 or 1 data byte, and a [Consumer](#type-consumer) accepts SYNC in CAN FD frames as well as classical ones (without the option it ignores CAN FD frames). The SYNC protocol itself is unchanged in CANopen FD (CiA's CANopen FD poster: SYNC with an optional 1-byte counter on CAN-ID 080h).

#### func WithHandler

```go
func WithHandler(h func(Event)) Option
```

WithHandler calls h for every SYNC a [Consumer](#type-consumer) receives, on its goroutine; h must not block for long (synchronous PDOs are due).

#### func WithOverflow


WithOverflow sets the synchronous counter overflow value: 0 (the default) sends SYNC without data, 2..240 adds a counter byte running from 1 to the value. A [Consumer](#type-consumer) given an overflow value checks the length of received SYNC messages.

### type Producer

```go
type Producer struct {
	// contains filtered or unexported fields
}
```

Producer is the SYNC producer (CiA 301 7.2.5): every communication cycle period it sends the SYNC message, with a counter byte when the counter overflow value is not 0. A new period takes effect at once and restarts the counter at 1.

With a dictionary it produces only while bit 30 (generate) of 0x1005 is set. Periods are kept by a time.Ticker: SYNC does not drift, but each message may be late by the scheduling latency of the Go runtime and the operating system (typically tens to hundreds of microseconds, more on a loaded system), so a Go SYNC producer suits cycle periods of milliseconds rather than tight motion control loops.
